Material tester · runs in your browser

Invent a material. Find out where it burns.

Spacecraft materials are approved with fire tests on Earth. The challenge asks whether a material that passes on Earth will keep burning in orbit, on the Moon or on Mars. Build a material from its chemistry, or blend existing ones, give it one Earth test, and FLINT predicts the least oxygen it needs on each world.

  1. 1 · Make itPick a known material, type its atoms, or blend two or three by mass.
  2. 2 · Test it on EarthEnter one measured oxygen limit. FLINT calibrates on it, as it did on NASA's tests.
  3. 3 · PredictRead its limit on four worlds, where it sits among NASA's materials, and send it into a cabin fire.

The physics underneath

The flammability map

Every material has a U-shaped map. At the left, the flow is too weak to feed the flame faster than it loses heat, so it starves. At the right, the flow outruns the chemistry and blows the flame off. Gravity sets where a cabin sits on the map, because rising hot gas is the only flow in still air. That is why the Moon is not simply "Earth with less fire".

How the prediction works, and its limits

  • Chemistry to flame temperature. From the atoms FLINT works out how much oxygen the material needs, its heat of combustion (Huggett's 13.1 MJ per kg of oxygen, unless you measured it) and its flame temperature in any oxygen level, with NIST-JANAF gas data.
  • Two ways to die. NASA's model (ICES-2025-392) says a flame dies when the flow blows it off or when it loses heat faster than it makes it. FLINT adds a flow speed for any gravity and pressure.
  • One Earth test calibrates it. The blow-off constant is set so FLINT reproduces your test exactly, the way FLINT was calibrated on NASA's 1-g tests and then predicted NASA's four lunar limits to within 1.4 points of oxygen on average.
  • Without a test it is an estimate. The flame chemistry is borrowed from acrylic, polycarbonate or Nomex. Pyrolysis temperatures for the non-NASA presets are typical values; replace them with your own.
  • What it does not cover. Thin solids spreading a flame upward in oxygen and nitrogen. Not thick parts, dripping, smouldering, fluorine or chlorine chemistry, or still air in orbit. It has not been reviewed by NASA and it is not a safety certification. Inspect the evidence and the Python engine.
